$comment: Inline-asm P5c (D-LIR-ASM-UNPINNED-INPUT-NEVER-MATERIALISED): the first runnable witness that an asm INPUT operand's VALUE reaches the template. ★★★ THIS EXAMPLE WAS BORN RED ON A COMPILER THAT PASSED 873/873. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-17 before the fix: `__asm__("movl %1, %0" : "=r"(r) : "r"(a))` with a == 42 compiled rc=0 and returned 0 on BOTH pe64-x86_64 and elf64-x86_64, at BOTH debug and release — `expandInlineAsm` moved only PINNED inputs into their bound registers and skipped the unpinned ones, so the template read a vreg nothing wrote. The corpus could not see it because its three inline-asm examples between them declared ZERO inputs: `c_inline_asm` is the empty template, and `c_inline_asm_extended` is pinned OUTPUTS on x86_64 and a pure CLOBBER list on aarch64. ⇒ coverage is as wide as the OPERAND SHAPES named, not as the example count. ★★★ WHY THE FILE CARRIES TWO OPERAND SHAPES — A MEASUREMENT, NOT A STYLE CHOICE. Reading an undefined register is undefined at EVERY optimization level, so the obvious expectation is that one input-shaped pin reddens every arm. ✘ WRONG, measured: with the mutant restored and the example reduced to the call-shaped two-input `dssAsmAdd` alone, baseline exited 42 (GREEN — the mutant SURVIVED, the allocator having left the right value in the register the template read) while release exited 1. Adding the single-input shape lowered directly in `main` made the same mutant fail the BASELINE arm outright (`baseline exit-code mismatch (expected=42; OS=1)`). ⇒ a pin that passes because an undefined register happened to hold the right value is not a pin, and which shape gets that luck cannot be read off the source. Both shapes stay; the `release` arm stays mandatory as the arm that proves the optimizer did not fold the input path away. ⚠ THE `volatile` SEED IS LOAD-BEARING: without it release folds the operands to constants before lowering, which does not make the pin vacuous but does silently change which mechanism each arm tests. ⚠ WHY THE aarch64 ARM USES `long`: `add %w0, %w1, %w2` is the natural 32-bit spelling and `%w` is an operand MODIFIER that no shipped target declares a width-view vocabulary for; the semantic tier refuses it fail-loud (D-CSUBSET-INLINE-ASM-OPERANDS) rather than running the op at the wrong width. Plain `%0` on 64-bit operands is the shape that is expressible today — measured, not assumed. When the modifier vocabulary lands, a `%w` arm belongs beside this one.
